method_card.title: How to read dynamic and articulation markings
method_card.content:
The AQA Listening exam regularly asks you to identify dynamic markings, articulation signs and performance directions from a score excerpt. This lesson covers all the markings you need to know.

Dynamics (volume):

  • pp (pianissimo) = very quiet
  • p (piano) = quiet
  • mp (mezzo-piano) = moderately quiet
  • mf (mezzo-forte) = moderately loud
  • f (forte) = loud
  • ff (fortissimo) = very loud
  • cresc. or ⟨ (crescendo) = gradually get louder
  • dim. or ⟩ (diminuendo/decrescendo) = gradually get quieter
  • sfz or sf (sforzando) = a sudden heavy accent on one note

Articulation:

  • Staccato: a dot above/below a note = play short and detached
  • Legato: a curved line (slur) over a group of notes = play smoothly and connected
  • Tenuto: a short dash above a note = hold for full value, slightly weighted
  • Accent (> or ^): emphasise this note
  • Fermata (𝄐): hold this note longer than its written value
steps: Scan the score for any letters below or above the staff — these are likely dynamic markings.
Look for curved lines spanning groups of notes — if they connect different pitches, they are slurs (legato); if they are over one note, they are a tie.
Look for dots above or below noteheads — these indicate staccato.
Look for hairpin symbols (⟨ ⟩) — these are crescendo and diminuendo.

bronze.question: Look at Excerpt A (Chopin Nocturne). What dynamic marking appears at the start of the piece?
options: ff (fortissimo)
mf (mezzo-forte)
p (piano)
pp (pianissimo)
bronze.explanation: The Nocturne opens with p (piano) — quiet. This gentle dynamic suits the intimate, nocturnal character of the piece. The direction 'espressivo' (expressively) often accompanies this marking in the score.

bronze.question: Look at Excerpt B (Beethoven Symphony No.1 Allegro). What does the marking 'sf' mean?
options: Slowly and calmly (senza fretta)
A sudden heavy accent on that note (sforzando)
Always play this passage softly (sempre forte)
A gradual diminuendo to silence
bronze.explanation: sf (or sfz, sforzando) means a sudden heavy accent on the marked note. It is not a dynamic level — the surrounding music can be at any dynamic. Beethoven uses sf accents extensively as a rhythmic and expressive device, particularly in fast Allegro passages.

bronze.question: Put the following dynamic markings in order from quietest to loudest.
bronze.explanation: The standard dynamic scale from quietest to loudest: pp → p → mp → mf → f → ff. (mp was not in this list but fits between p and mf.) Knowing this order is essential for any score-reading question that asks about dynamic contrasts.

silver.question: Look at Excerpt A (Chopin Nocturne). The melody has a long curved line spanning many notes. What does this indicate?
options: A tie — the two notes on either end are the same pitch and should be held as one long note.
A slur — the notes within the curve should be played smoothly and connected (legato).
A trill — rapid alternation between two notes.
A glissando — slide continuously between the first and last note.
silver.explanation: A slur is a curved line over a group of different pitches, indicating legato (smooth, connected) playing. Ties look similar but connect two notes of the same pitch. In the Nocturne, the long slurs over the melody tell the pianist to play without breaks between notes — creating the smooth, singing quality of the piece.

silver.question: Look at Excerpt B (Beethoven Symphony No.1 Allegro). What symbol indicates a gradual increase in volume?
options: A dot above the notehead (staccato)
A short horizontal dash above the notehead (tenuto)
A hairpin opening to the right (⟨) — a crescendo
The letter 'p' below the staff
silver.explanation: The hairpin crescendo symbol (⟨) shows a gradual increase in volume from the left end to the right end of the symbol. The wider end indicates where the music is loudest. Beethoven uses this in the Allegro to build energy towards climaxes.

silver.question: Match each articulation marking to what it tells the performer to do.

pairs.right: Tenuto — hold for full value, slightly weighted

pairs.left: Symbol '>' above or below a note

pairs.right: Fermata (pause) — hold longer than written value

silver.explanation: These five articulation symbols are the most common in GCSE-level scores. Identifying them correctly is worth 1 mark each in the exam. The slur and tie look similar — remember that a slur spans different pitches; a tie connects the same pitch.

gold.question: In Excerpt B (Beethoven Symphony No.1 Allegro), sf marks appear frequently. How does sforzando differ from simply marking a note forte (f)?
options: They are identical — sf and f mean the same thing.
f is a dynamic level that applies to a whole passage; sf is a momentary, sudden heavy accent on a single note regardless of the surrounding dynamic level.
sf means the whole orchestra gets louder, whereas f means only the strings get louder.
sf tells the performer to gradually get louder; f tells them to stay at the same volume.
gold.explanation: Forte (f) is a dynamic level — it applies continuously to the surrounding passage. Sforzando (sf/sfz) is an articulation accent: a sudden, sharp emphasis on a single note that can occur at any dynamic level, even in a pp passage. Beethoven's use of sf in the Allegro creates unexpected rhythmic stresses that give his music its characteristic driving energy.

gold.question: Compare Excerpts A (Chopin, legato) and C (Mozart, phrase slurs with dynamic contrast). How do the articulation markings reflect the different styles of these composers?
options: Both composers use identical articulation techniques — there is no stylistic difference.

Chopin's long legato slurs and quiet dynamics reflect Romantic lyrical expression; Mozart's shorter phrase slurs with sudden dynamic contrasts (p to f) reflect Classical phrase structure and terraced dynamics.
Mozart uses more legato slurs than Chopin; Chopin uses sforzando accents throughout.
Chopin writes in forte throughout; Mozart writes entirely in pianissimo.
gold.explanation: The articulation markings reflect the composers' different styles. Chopin's Romantic piano writing uses long, singing legato slurs and predominantly quiet, nuanced dynamics. Mozart's Classical symphony uses shorter slurs that define phrase shapes and employs terraced dynamics (sudden jumps from p to f) rather than gradual hairpins. Reading the markings tells you not just how to play, but something about the era and style of the music.

worked_examples.question: Look at Excerpt B (Beethoven Symphony No.1 Allegro). Identify two markings from the score and explain the effect each has in performance.
steps: Step 1 — spot the sf marks. The letters 'sf' appear below certain notes. This is sforzando: a sudden heavy accent on that single note. Effect: creates unexpected rhythmic stresses that drive the music and add urgency.
Step 2 — spot the crescendo hairpin. The opening hairpin symbol (⟨) shows a gradual increase in volume. Effect: builds tension and energy toward a fortissimo climax.

Full answer. 'sf (sforzando) marks: these indicate a sudden heavy accent on individual notes (1 mark), giving the passage a jagged, energetic character (1 mark). Crescendo hairpin (⟨): this gradual increase in volume (1 mark) builds tension and drives toward the fortissimo climax (1 mark).'
